newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Hong Kong's hot red chips seen pausing for review.
newsitem.headline: Hong Kong's hot red chips seen pausing for review.

text.p: China-related stocks will remain a major investment theme ahead of Hong Kong's reversion to China, but fears that Beijing may exert some control over the sector has cooled the inflow of money, analysts say.

"If red chips continued to rise as they did on Thursday and Friday last week, they (China's authorities) definitely will take action," said one Hong Kong-based China analyst with a large European brokerage.
Some brokers said they turned net sellers last Friday on concerns China would take steps to cool the speculation in red chips.
"The gains last week were very unreasonable," said China analyst An Lu at Salomon Brothers.

Red chips are Hong Kong-based companies with mainland Chinese parents, often ministries or government-backed firms, and buying has been driven by hopes the parents would inject inexpensive mainland assets into the Hong Kong units.

Last week, China Merchants Hai Hong Holdings Ltd led the sector with a jump of 41.34 percent. China Everbright IHD Pacific Ltd put on 18.84 percent and Shanghai Industrial Holdings Ltd added 9.14 percent.
Their performance this week has been more mixed, with many favourites hit by profit-taking on Monday and Tuesday but rebounding on Wednesday in line with a blue-chip led rally.
"We could see from the turnover figures that there was overspeculation in red chips," said Amy Wong, research director at New China Hong Kong.
In the Monday morning session in particular, when turnover totalled about HK$8.0 billion, about HK$6.0 billion was trade in red chips, Wong said.
But analysts said overspeculation did not warrant shunning all red chips.
"We like the China growth story and we will continue to focus on quality red chips," added Wong.
Gains in red chip prices over the first four months of the year have been astounding, brokers and analysts said.

While Chinese authorities may be loathe to see these shares spiral out of sight, they were also likely to be hesitant about being heavy-handed or interfering in Hong Kong's jurisdiction, analysts said.

The China Securities Regulatory Commission (CSRC), China's securities' markets watchdog, and other financial regulators have repeatedly said they would not interfere in supervisory matters in Hong Kong, in keeping with Beijing's promise to allow the territory a high degree of autonomy after the handover.

Analysts said measures open to the Chinese government include letting market forces play a greater role by allowing more Chinese companies to list their Hong Kong units and thereby creating a steady supply of good quality investment vehicles.
Another tool would be moral suasion, as in talking the market down. The authorities have used this method very effectively on domestic markets in China.
Beijing was also working on strengthening the domestic legal framework, including clearer guidelines on the sale, pricing and ownership of national property, analysts said.

"Right now there is no approval process for the red chips, it is just ad hoc," said a China analyst at a U.S. brokerage. "But I think investors are going to begin asking more about the process of asset injection."
